q: A financial appraisal that projects a project's earnings and working expenses at constant (today's) prices and levels over a long life, with no allowance for the growth of traffic or the escalation of working expenses, is open to the objection that:

options.A: It always understates the return of the project
options.B: It treats the discount rate as zero
options.C: It ignores the payback period of the project
options.D: Its projected return may be misleading, since earnings and working expenses in practice change over the life of the project and a realistic appraisal must provide for such changes

q: Under the certainty-equivalent method of handling risk in project appraisal:

options.A: The expected cash flows are first reduced to their certainty equivalents (the certain amounts considered equally desirable) and these are then discounted at the risk-free rate
options.B: The cash flows are discounted at a rate higher than the cost of capital
options.C: Only the most pessimistic cash flow estimate is used, without any discounting
options.D: The payback period is shortened by a fixed margin for every project

q: In the financial justification of a work, only those earnings and expenses that are attributable to the work itself are taken into account. This follows the principle that appraisal is concerned with:

options.A: The total earnings of the railway as a whole
options.B: Incremental (additional) earnings and incremental working expenses arising from the work, common system costs not affected by the work being excluded
options.C: The earnings of the work in its first year only
options.D: The book value of the assets already existing on the section

q: The net profit after tax of an enterprise is Rs 3,40,000 and its net sales are Rs 20,00,000. Its net profit ratio is:
The net sales of an enterprise are Rs 28,00,000 and its operating profit is Rs 5,60,000. Its operating profit ratio is:
Operating profit differs from net profit (after tax) of an enterprise in that operating profit:

options.A: Is computed before deducting the cost of goods sold
options.B: Includes profit on the sale of fixed assets and other non-operating income
options.C: Is always larger than the gross profit of the enterprise
options.D: Is earned from the normal operations of the enterprise and excludes non-operating incomes and expenses, interest and tax

q: The office and administration expenses of an enterprise are Rs 1,44,000 and its net sales are Rs 24,00,000. Its office and administration expense ratio is:
Ratios of an enterprise can be meaningfully compared with those of other enterprises in the same industry (inter-firm comparison) only when:

options.A: The enterprises have identical sales volumes
options.B: The enterprises follow broadly uniform accounting policies and the ratios relate to the same period
options.C: The enterprises are located in the same city
options.D: The enterprises have the same number of employees

q: The profit after tax of an enterprise is Rs 5,20,000 and its total assets are Rs 40,00,000. Its return on assets is:
In the three-factor DuPont decomposition, the Return on Equity is expressed as the product of:

options.A: The current ratio, the debt-equity ratio and the interest coverage ratio
options.B: The gross profit ratio, the net profit ratio and the operating ratio
options.C: The net profit margin, the total assets turnover and the equity multiplier (assets divided by equity)
options.D: The inventory turnover, the debtors turnover and the creditors turnover

q: An enterprise has a net profit margin of 8%, a total assets turnover of 2.5 times and an equity multiplier of 2. Its Return on Equity, on the DuPont decomposition, is:
A serious limitation of ratio analysis arising from the historical-cost basis of accounts is that:

options.A: Ratios cannot be expressed as percentages
options.B: Ratios ignore changes in the price level over time, so comparisons of ratios over a long period, or between firms holding assets bought at very different price levels, can be distorted
options.C: Ratios can be computed only at the end of the financial year
options.D: Ratios require the enterprise to be listed on a stock exchange

q: A company's share is quoted in the market at Rs 135 and its Earnings Per Share is Rs 15. Its price-earnings (P/E) ratio is:
A comparatively high price-earnings ratio of a company's share generally indicates that:

options.A: The company is about to be wound up
options.B: The market price is low in relation to the current earnings per share
options.C: Investors are paying a high price for each rupee of current earnings, usually in expectation of higher future earnings growth
options.D: The company declares a very high dividend

q: A company declares a Dividend Per Share of Rs 12 while its share is quoted in the market at Rs 150. Its dividend yield is:
The total dividend declared by a company for the year is Rs 3,50,000 and its net profit after tax is Rs 10,00,000. Its dividend payout ratio is:
The earnings retained by a company (the portion of profit not distributed as dividend) are significant for its finances mainly because they:

options.A: Have to be repaid to the shareholders on demand
options.B: Provide an internal source of funds for expansion and modernisation without raising outside capital
options.C: Reduce the market price of the company's shares immediately
options.D: Are kept as cash in hand at all times

q: The net sales of an enterprise are Rs 38,50,000 and the net working capital employed by it is Rs 7,00,000. Its working capital turnover ratio is:

options.A: 0.18 times
options.B: 5 times
options.C: 5.5 times
options.D: 6.5 times

q: An excessively high working capital turnover ratio of an enterprise may be a warning sign because it can indicate:

options.A: That the enterprise holds too much idle cash
options.B: Overtrading, that is, carrying on a large volume of business on an inadequate working capital base, exposing it to liquidity strain
options.C: That the enterprise has no debtors
options.D: That the enterprise is earning no profit

q: The annual credit purchases of an enterprise are Rs 18,25,000 and its average trade creditors are Rs 2,50,000. The average period of credit it enjoys from its suppliers (on a 365-day year) is:

options.A: 50 days
options.B: 7.3 days
options.C: 45 days
options.D: 60 days

q: A steady lengthening, over the years, of the average payment period taken by an enterprise to pay its trade creditors, well beyond the credit terms agreed with suppliers, generally suggests:

options.A: Improving liquidity and prompt payment discipline
options.B: That the enterprise has stopped purchasing on credit
options.C: Liquidity strain, with payments being stretched, which may damage supplier relations and the enterprise's credit standing
options.D: That the creditors turnover ratio has risen

q: A company has preference share capital of Rs 5,00,000, debentures and long-term loans of Rs 10,00,000 and equity shareholders' funds of Rs 10,00,000. Its capital gearing ratio (fixed-cost capital to equity shareholders' funds) is:
Over five years, an enterprise's debt ratio has risen steadily while its interest coverage ratio has fallen steadily. Taken together, these trends indicate that:

options.A: Its long-term solvency is strengthening and its financial risk is falling
options.B: Its liquidity position alone has improved
options.C: It has repaid most of its long-term borrowings
options.D: Its long-term solvency is weakening and its financial risk is increasing, as a growing share of its assets is financed by debt while its earnings cover its interest charges less comfortably

q: In a common-size (vertical) statement, each item is expressed as a percentage of:

options.A: The corresponding item of the base year
options.B: The net profit of the enterprise
options.C: A common base for that statement, such as net sales in the profit and loss account or total assets (total liabilities) in the balance sheet, for the same period
options.D: The corresponding item of another enterprise

q: Trend analysis of financial statements differs from common-size analysis in that trend analysis:

options.A: Expresses each item of a year as a percentage of a common base of the same year
options.B: Takes a selected base year as 100 and expresses the corresponding items of other years as percentages (indices) of the base-year figures, showing the direction and rate of change over time
options.C: Compares the enterprise with the industry average of a single year
options.D: Is confined to the balance sheet only

q: Budgetary control is sometimes described as a system which combines:

options.A: Centralisation of both responsibility and control in the top management
options.B: Decentralisation of responsibility for achieving the targets with centralisation of control through budgets and performance reports
options.C: Complete freedom for each department, with no central control at all
options.D: Control only over cash receipts and payments of the enterprise

q: In a factory, the available plant capacity is the factor that limits the level of activity, all other factors being adequate. In such a case, the functional budgets will have to be built around the:

options.A: Production budget, which becomes the starting point because plant capacity is the principal budget factor
options.B: Cash budget, which is always prepared first in every enterprise
options.C: Selling overhead budget of the marketing department
options.D: Research and development budget of the enterprise

q: Regarding the revision of budgets during the budget period, the correct position is that:

options.A: A budget should never be revised, whatever changes may occur in the conditions assumed
options.B: A budget should be revised every week so that it always agrees with the latest actuals
options.C: A budget should be revised when the assumptions on which it rests have changed materially, but too frequent revision weakens its value as a standard for control
options.D: Revision of the budget is required only when the actual results are favourable

q: A budget provides for fixed costs of Rs 2,70,000 and variable costs of Rs 16 per unit. The total flexed budget allowance for an actual output of 22,500 units is:
The preparation of a flexible budget is possible only when the costs of the enterprise are:

options.A: Recorded separately in the financial accounts and the cost accounts
options.B: Classified according to their behaviour into fixed, semi-variable and variable costs, the semi-variable costs being further split into their fixed and variable elements
options.C: Charged wholly to the products manufactured during the period
options.D: Approved in advance by the budget committee of the enterprise

q: The output of a department was budgeted at 50,000 units, but the actual output was only 40,000 units. For a fair comparison of the actual costs of the department with the budget for the purpose of control, the management should compare the actual costs with:

options.A: The original budget prepared for 50,000 units, without any adjustment
options.B: The budget of the corresponding month of the previous year
options.C: The average cost of similar departments in other enterprises
options.D: The flexed budget recast for the actual level of activity of 40,000 units

q: Budgeted sales of a product are 72,000 units. The opening stock of finished goods is 9,000 units and the closing stock is to be raised to 12,000 units. The production budget should provide for production of:

options.A: 75,000 units
options.B: 69,000 units
options.C: 72,000 units
options.D: 81,000 units

q: In Zero-Based Budgeting, after the decision units of the organisation have been identified, the next step in the process is:

options.A: Ranking of all the decision packages of the enterprise in order of priority
options.B: Formulation of decision packages by the managers of the decision units, setting out the cost, benefits and consequences of each activity
options.C: Allocation of the available funds to the approved packages
options.D: Preparation of the budgeted profit and loss account of the enterprise

q: Under Zero-Based Budgeting, the decision packages of all the units are ranked and the available funds are allotted in the order of priority. The practical consequence of this ranking is that:

options.A: Packages falling below the cut-off line up to which funds are available receive no allotment, even though the activity concerned may have been carried on for many years
options.B: Every activity of the enterprise is funded at least at the level of the previous year
options.C: Funds are divided equally among all the departments of the enterprise
options.D: Only the new activities proposed during the year are ranked, the old activities being funded automatically

q: A performance budget presents the budget of an organisation primarily in terms of:

options.A: The objects of expenditure, such as salaries, travel and contingencies
options.B: The sources from which the funds are to be raised
options.C: Functions, programmes and activities or projects, together with the physical targets to be achieved under each of them
options.D: The cash receipts and payments expected during the year

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. A traditional line-item budget classifies the proposed expenditure by objects, such as salaries, wages and travelling expenses, without linking it to the work to be performed.
2. A performance budget classifies the expenditure by activities and programmes and links it to the physical outputs to be achieved.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Neither 1 nor 2
options.D: Both 1 and 2

q: Budgetary control differs from standard costing mainly in that:

options.A: Budgetary control is concerned only with the production department, while standard costing covers the whole enterprise
options.B: Budgetary control embraces the operations of the whole enterprise, including sales, production, administration and finance, while standard costing is concerned mainly with the elements of cost of products or services
options.C: Standard costing is a technique of long-term planning, while budgetary control relates only to cash
options.D: There is no difference at all between the two techniques

q: Through the budget, the plans, policies and targets approved by the top management are conveyed to the managers at the operating levels, and the results achieved are reported back through the budgetary reports. This highlights the role of budgets as a means of:

options.A: Valuing the closing stock of the enterprise
options.B: Fixing the selling prices of the products
options.C: Communication and coordination within the organisation
options.D: Computing the tax liability of the enterprise

q: A cost which a responsibility centre manager cannot influence during a short period, such as the rent payable under a lease already entered into, may still become controllable by him over a longer period when the lease comes up for renewal. This illustrates that, under responsibility accounting, controllability of a cost depends on:

options.A: The amount of the cost involved
options.B: Whether the cost is a fixed cost or a variable cost
options.C: The department in which the cost is recorded
options.D: The length of the period over which the performance of the manager is judged

q: In a well-designed system of responsibility accounting, the performance reports are so arranged that:

options.A: Every report contains the full details of all the transactions of the enterprise
options.B: Reports are prepared only for the top management and not for the lower levels
options.C: Each manager receives only the reports of the other departments
options.D: The reports are progressively summarised as they move up the levels of management, the report at each higher level covering in summary form the results of the centres below it

q:
Consider the following statements about the concepts of working capital:
1. Gross working capital is described as the quantitative concept, because it looks at the total amount invested in current assets.
2. Net working capital is described as the qualitative concept, because it indicates the extent to which current assets are financed by long-term funds.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Both 1 and 2
options.D: Neither 1 nor 2

q: In a manufacturing concern, raw materials are held for 36 days, the production process takes 18 days, finished goods are held for 24 days and debtors are collected in 42 days. Suppliers allow 30 days' credit. The length of the net operating cycle is:

options.A: 120 days
options.B: 90 days
options.C: 84 days
options.D: 150 days

q: The annual operating cost of an enterprise is Rs 43,20,000, reckoning a year of 360 days. Its operating cycle is 72 days. On the operating-cycle method, the working capital required is:
A growing enterprise whose sales increase steadily from year to year will need additional working capital even if the length of its operating cycle remains unchanged, mainly because:

options.A: The scale of its current assets, such as stock and debtors, rises with the higher volume of business, requiring more funds to be locked up in them
options.B: Its fixed costs go on increasing every year
options.C: Its suppliers stop giving it any credit
options.D: Its current liabilities rise faster than its current assets

q: A trading firm sells almost entirely for cash, turns over its stock rapidly and obtains long credit from its suppliers. Its own working capital requirement will be comparatively small mainly because:

options.A: It does not maintain any current assets at all
options.B: A large part of its operating cycle is financed by the suppliers through trade credit, and very little of its own funds remains locked up in debtors
options.C: It is exempt from maintaining a cash balance
options.D: Its current liabilities are always equal to its current assets

q: Which of the following is a long-term source of financing working capital?

options.A: Trade credit obtained from the suppliers of materials
options.B: Cash credit obtained from the bank against hypothecation of stock
options.C: Commercial paper issued in the money market
options.D: Retained earnings, that is, profits ploughed back into the business

q: Under the projected balance sheet method of estimating working capital, the requirement is worked out by:

options.A: Preparing a projected balance sheet for the budget period after estimating each item of current assets and current liabilities, the working capital being reflected in the balance of the projected position
options.B: Applying a fixed percentage to the fixed assets of the enterprise
options.C: Taking the working capital of a similar enterprise as the requirement
options.D: Dividing the annual operating cost by the current ratio of the enterprise

q: A seasonal enterprise requires working capital of Rs 4,00,000 at the lowest point of its activity during the year and Rs 11,00,000 at the seasonal peak. In terms of permanent and temporary working capital:

options.A: Its permanent working capital is Rs 11,00,000 and its temporary working capital is nil
options.B: Its permanent working capital is Rs 7,00,000 and its temporary working capital is Rs 4,00,000
options.C: Its permanent working capital is Rs 4,00,000 and its temporary working capital at the peak is Rs 7,00,000
options.D: The whole of its working capital is temporary, since its level keeps changing

q: An enterprise which persistently carries inadequate working capital is likely to:

options.A: Earn cash discounts regularly on all its purchases
options.B: Enjoy the highest credit standing in the market
options.C: Hold excessive stocks of slow-moving materials
options.D: Fail to pay its creditors on the due dates, forgo cash discounts and damage its credit standing and relations with suppliers

q: An enterprise has an inventory conversion period of 64 days, a receivables collection period of 36 days and a payables deferral period of 28 days. Its cash conversion cycle is:

options.A: 72 days
options.B: 100 days
options.C: 56 days
options.D: 128 days

q: The management of an enterprise tightens its credit standards, granting credit only to financially strong customers and insisting on stricter screening. The most likely overall effect of this change is that:

options.A: Sales will rise sharply and bad debts will also rise
options.B: The investment in receivables will increase considerably
options.C: Sales may decline somewhat, but bad debts, collection costs and the funds blocked in receivables will fall
options.D: There will be no effect at all on sales or on receivables

q:
Consider the following statements regarding inventory as a part of working capital:
1. Buying materials in larger lots reduces the ordering costs and the risk of stock-outs interrupting production.
2. Buying materials in larger lots raises the average stock held, blocking more working capital and increasing the carrying costs.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Neither 1 nor 2
options.D: Both 1 and 2

q: In budgetary control, the budgeted working days of a department for a period are 300 and the actual working days are 288. The calendar ratio of the department is:
Depreciation charged in the profit and loss account is added back to the net profit in computing the funds from operations. This is done because:

options.A: Depreciation is a cash expense of the year
options.B: Depreciation creates a separate fund of cash in the business
options.C: Depreciation is a non-cash charge which does not involve any outflow of funds, and it is added back only to cancel its effect on the reported profit; by itself it generates no funds
options.D: Depreciation represents the profit earned on the fixed assets

q: The net profit of an enterprise is Rs 2,00,000, after charging depreciation of Rs 50,000 and preliminary expenses written off of Rs 15,000, and after crediting a profit of Rs 25,000 on the sale of land. The funds from operations are:
A transaction gives rise to a flow of funds, that is, a change in working capital, only when:

options.A: It involves a cash account on one side
options.B: It affects one current account and one non-current account, transactions wholly within current accounts or wholly within non-current accounts causing no flow
options.C: It is recorded in the profit and loss account of the enterprise
options.D: It takes place in the second half of the financial year

q: An enterprise raises a fresh long-term loan and uses the entire proceeds to repay an existing long-term loan. In its fund flow statement, this will appear as:

options.A: Both a source of funds (the fresh loan raised) and an application of funds (the old loan repaid), the net working capital remaining unchanged
options.B: Neither a source nor an application of funds
options.C: A source of funds only, equal to the fresh loan raised
options.D: An application of funds only, equal to the old loan repaid

q: The current assets of an enterprise increased from Rs 6,40,000 to Rs 7,30,000 during a year, while its current liabilities increased from Rs 3,80,000 to Rs 4,10,000. The net change in its working capital during the year is:

options.A: An increase of Rs 90,000
options.B: A decrease of Rs 60,000
options.C: An increase of Rs 60,000
options.D: An increase of Rs 30,000

q: An enterprise's operating profit before working capital changes is Rs 4,80,000. During the year, its stock decreased by Rs 30,000, its debtors increased by Rs 55,000 and its creditors decreased by Rs 20,000. The cash from operations is:
A fund flow statement of an enterprise may show a healthy increase in working capital during a year, and yet the enterprise may face an acute shortage of cash in the same year, because:

options.A: The fund flow statement is always prepared incorrectly
options.B: Depreciation is not charged in the profit and loss account
options.C: The increase in working capital is measured only in terms of cash
options.D: The additional funds may have got locked up in larger stocks and debtors, so that working capital has risen while the cash position has worsened

q: As regards the statutory position of the two statements, it is correct to say that:

options.A: The preparation of a cash flow statement is required under Accounting Standard 3 (AS-3) or Ind AS 7 for the specified enterprises, whereas the fund flow statement is not statutorily required and is prepared voluntarily for management purposes
options.B: The fund flow statement is compulsory under the Companies Act, whereas the cash flow statement is voluntary
options.C: Both the statements are compulsory for every enterprise, big or small
options.D: Neither of the two statements can be prepared by a government department

q: In preparing a cash flow statement by the indirect method, the cash flow from operating activities is computed by starting with:

options.A: The closing balance of cash and cash equivalents
options.B: The net profit before tax and extraordinary items, adjusted for non-cash and non-operating items and thereafter for changes in the working capital items
options.C: The gross sales of the enterprise for the year
options.D: The funds from operations as shown in the fund flow statement

q: A supplier offers credit terms of 2/10, net 60, that is, a cash discount of 2% for payment within 10 days, the full amount being otherwise payable in 60 days. The approximate annual cost of not taking the cash discount, on a 360-day year basis, is:
In a Value Added Statement, the value added by an enterprise is computed as:

options.A: The net profit after tax earned by the enterprise
options.B: The total of wages, salaries and bonus paid to the employees
options.C: The value of its output (sales and other income) minus the cost of the materials and services bought in from outside suppliers, the statement then showing how this wealth created is distributed among employees, government, providers of capital and retention in the business
options.D: The excess of the market value of the enterprise over its book value

q: Social accounting is mainly concerned with:

options.A: Preparing the accounts of clubs and other non-trading concerns
options.B: Measuring and reporting the social costs and social benefits of the activities of an enterprise, that is, its effect on the society and the environment, in addition to its financial results
options.C: Computing the social welfare contribution payable by the employees
options.D: Maintaining the provident fund accounts of the staff

q: A social audit of an enterprise means:

options.A: A systematic evaluation and verification of the social performance of the enterprise against its stated social objectives and the expectations of the society
options.B: The statutory audit of the accounts of a co-operative society
options.C: An audit of the entertainment expenditure incurred by the officers
options.D: An inspection of the welfare amenities provided in the office canteen

q: Historical cost accounts become misleading during a period of rising prices mainly because:

options.A: The depreciation charged on the historical cost of assets is lower than the cost of using those assets at current prices, so that the reported profit is overstated and may be distributed, impairing the capital of the enterprise
options.B: The sales of the enterprise are recorded at prices lower than the market prices
options.C: The creditors of the enterprise are shown at more than the amounts payable to them
options.D: Cash and bank balances lose their value in the balance sheet

q: For budgetary control to work, the accounting system of the enterprise must be so organised that:

options.A: The accounts are maintained only in summary form by the head office
options.B: The classification of accounts corresponds to the budget centres and budget heads, so that the actual results can be collected and compared promptly with the corresponding budgets
options.C: A separate set of books is maintained for every budget
options.D: The actual results are compiled only after the close of the financial year

q: Working capital is also called the circulating or revolving capital of an enterprise because:

options.A: It is contributed by the shareholders in rotation
options.B: The bank reviews the cash credit limit every year
options.C: It is invested only in the cash balance of the enterprise
options.D: The funds invested in current assets keep circulating through the operating cycle, changing their form from cash to materials, work-in-progress, finished goods and debtors, and back into cash

q: For planning purposes, the fund flow statement is generally more useful than the cash flow statement when management is concerned with:

options.A: The cash balance expected at the end of the next week
options.B: Long-term financial planning, such as assessing how the expansion of the enterprise has been financed and what structural changes have taken place in its financial position
options.C: Deciding the denominations of currency to be kept in the office chest
options.D: Verifying the bank balance on a particular day

q:
Consider the following statements:
1. Defectives are units that fall short of the prescribed standard of quality but can be rectified by incurring additional material, labour or overhead cost and then disposed of as good units or as seconds.
2. Spoilage refers to units that are damaged beyond rectification and can be sold only for their scrap or disposal value.
Which of the statements is/are correct?

options.A: 1 only
options.B: 2 only
options.C: Neither 1 nor 2
options.D: Both 1 and 2

q: Which of the following items is normally EXCLUDED from cost accounts, being treated as a purely financial matter or an appropriation of profit?

options.A: Depreciation of factory plant
options.B: Rent of the factory building
options.C: Income tax paid by the enterprise
options.D: Direct material consumed in production

q: Batch costing is most appropriately applied where:

options.A: A single non-repetitive job is executed to a customer's specific order
options.B: Production is carried out in batches, each batch is treated as a cost unit, and the cost per unit is obtained by dividing the total cost of the batch by the number of units in it
options.C: A liquid is passed through a series of continuous processes
options.D: Identical services are rendered to the public at large

q: In process costing, 'equivalent units' (equivalent production) means:

options.A: Partially completed units expressed in terms of fully completed units, according to the degree of completion reached for each element of cost
options.B: The number of units lost as normal loss in a process
options.C: The number of units transferred to the finished stock warehouse
options.D: Units of two different products treated as equal in selling price

q: The cost of normal idle time of workers — the unavoidable loss of time in setting up machines, changing tools or moving between jobs — is treated in cost accounts by:

options.A: Charging it in full to the Costing Profit and Loss Account as an abnormal loss
options.B: Ignoring it altogether, since no wages are paid for it
options.C: Treating it as part of the production cost, recovered through factory overheads or by inflating the hourly labour rate
options.D: Deducting it from the wages payable to the workers concerned

q: Under a perpetual inventory system, physical verification of stores can be carried out by continuous stock-taking mainly because:

options.A: The stores are closed down for a week at the end of every month
options.B: No record of receipts and issues is maintained in the stores
options.C: Stock is verified only once in three years by external auditors
options.D: The bin cards and stores ledger are written up after every receipt and issue, so balances are known at any moment and items can be checked in rotation without stopping work

q: An 'engineered cost centre', as distinct from a discretionary cost centre, is a responsibility centre in which:

options.A: The manager is responsible only for revenues earned
options.B: Output can be measured in physical or monetary terms and a clear, well-defined relationship exists between the inputs consumed and the output produced, as in a machining department
options.C: No budget can be prepared for the centre at all
options.D: The costs incurred are wholly uncontrollable by the manager

q: The maximum consumption of a material is 350 units per week and the maximum re-order period (lead time) is 4 weeks. The re-order level of the material is:

options.A: 1,400 units
options.B: 1,000 units
options.C: 1,050 units
options.D: 1,750 units

q: The re-order level of a material is 2,400 units and the re-order quantity is 1,500 units. Minimum consumption is 200 units per week and the minimum re-order period is 5 weeks. The maximum stock level is:

options.A: 3,900 units
options.B: 3,400 units
options.C: 2,900 units
options.D: 2,400 units

q: The re-order level of a material is 1,800 units. Normal consumption is 250 units per week and the normal re-order period is 4 weeks. The minimum stock level is:

options.A: 1,800 units
options.B: 800 units
options.C: 1,000 units
options.D: 550 units

q: The minimum stock level of a material is 650 units and the re-order quantity is 1,700 units. Using the formula: minimum level + one-half of the re-order quantity, the average stock level is:

options.A: 650 units
options.B: 850 units
options.C: 2,350 units
options.D: 1,500 units

q: The annual consumption of a material is 12,500 units. The cost of placing an order is Rs 50 and the carrying cost is Rs 5 per unit per year. Using EOQ = sqrt(2AO/C), the Economic Order Quantity is:

options.A: 500 units
options.B: 354 units
options.C: 707 units
options.D: 1,000 units

q: The standard wage rate is Rs 80 per hour and the actual rate paid is Rs 75 per hour. Actual hours worked are 3,000. The labour rate variance is:

options.A: Rs 15,000 (Adverse)
options.B: Rs 5,000 (Favourable)
options.C: Rs 15,000 (Favourable)
options.D: Rs 2,40,000 (Favourable)

q: Workers were paid for 1,800 hours, out of which 1,650 hours were actually productive, the balance being abnormal idle time. The standard wage rate is Rs 60 per hour. The idle time variance is:

options.A: Rs 9,000 (Favourable)
options.B: Rs 9,000 (Adverse)
options.C: Rs 1,08,000 (Adverse)
options.D: Rs 99,000 (Adverse)
